title: Linearization and Differentials
subtitle: Approximating a function with its tangent line

slides.title: Real functions are messy
slides.text: Here is a messy function, and its tangent line at the dot. Nobody wants to compute with the curve. Zoom in on the dot until you can't tell the two apart.
slides.after: Up close, the curve and its tangent line are basically the same. Lines are easy to work with. That's the whole idea.

slides.text: So, close to the point, we can swap the messy function for…
slides.hint: What did the curve turn into when you zoomed in?
slides.explain: Near the point, the tangent line is an excellent stand-in. Stray far away and you can make a new tangent line closer to where you are.

slides.text:
The **linearization** of $f$ at $x = a$ is
$L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$
What is $L(x)$, really?
options: The tangent line at $a$, written as a function
slides.hint: Compare it to point-slope form, $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.
slides.explain: **Nothing new!** It is the tangent line in point-slope form, solved for $y$. "Linearization" is just a fancy name for it.

slides.title: Label the pieces
slides.text:
$L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$
Match each piece with what it means.
pairs: the $x$-value where the line touches the curve
the height of the curve at that point
the slope of the tangent line
the input you want to estimate at
the estimate: height of the tangent line at $x$
slides.explain: Point $(a, f(a))$, slope $f'(a)$: that's a line. Plug in $x$ to get the estimate $L(x)$.

slides.text: Find the linearization of $f(x) = frac{1}{x}$ at $a = 2$. Start with the two numbers you need.
slides.title: Example

slides.text: So the linearization of $1/x$ at $a = 2$ is…
Use it to estimate $frac{1}{2.1}$: find $L(2.1)$.
slides.label: $L(2.1)$ =

slides.title: How close was it?
slides.text: The curve is $1/x$; the teal line is $L(x)$. Drag $x$ to 2.1 and compare the two heights.
slides.after: At $x$ = 2.1: $f$ = 0.47619 and $L$ = 0.475. Off by about 0.0012. Not bad for no calculator.

slides.text: You want to approximate $sqrt(9.1)$ with a linearization. Which function and point?
slides.hint: Pick $a$ close to 9.1 where $f(a)$ is easy to compute.
slides.explain: √9 = 3 is easy, and 9 is close to 9.1. (At 9.1 you'd need the answer to get the answer.)

slides.text: Approximate $sqrt(9.1)$ using $f(x) = sqrt(x)$ at $a = 9$.
Next: approximate $sin(62°)$, using $a = 60° = pi/3$. Before using the formula, the 2° step has to be converted to radians. Why?
options: The rule $(sin x)' = cos x$ only works in radians
slides.explain: The derivative $cos x$ assumes radians. So $x - a$ = 2° = $2pi/180$ = $pi/90$ ≈ 0.0349.

slides.text: $f(x) = sin x$, $a = pi/3$: $f(a) = sqrt(3)/2 ≈ 0.866025$ and $f'(a) = cos(pi/3) = 1/2$. Use the calculator.
Try: approximate $3.1^3$ with a linearization at $a = 3$.
slides.title: Try
How far can you trust it?
slides.text: $f(x) = sqrt(x)$ with its linearization at $a = 9$. Drag $x$ away from 9 and watch the error (red). When it passes 0.05, make a new linearization where you are.
slides.after: New point, new tangent line, tiny error again. If you have to go far from your point, just make a new linearization closer to where you need it.

slides.title: Differentials
slides.text: We know dy/dx = f′(x). Now treat dx and dy as two separate small numbers and multiply across:  dy = ___ · dx
slides.hint: Multiply both sides of $frac{dy}{dx} = f'(x)$ by $dx$.
slides.explain: $dy = f'(x) dx$. That's the definition of the differential $dy$.

slides.text: Three quantities. Match each to its meaning.
pairs: a small change in $x$ that you choose (same as $Δx$)
the real change in $f$: $f(x + dx) - f(x)$
the change along the tangent line: $f'(x) dx$
slides.hint: One of them uses the curve, one uses the tangent line.
slides.explain: $Δy$ follows the curve. $dy$ follows the tangent line. For small $dx$ they are almost equal.

slides.title: See dy and Δy
slides.text: Start at the dot. Move right by $dx$, then go up two ways: to the tangent line and to the curve.
slides.after: For small $dx$, $dy$ is a great approximation of $Δy$, and $dy = f'(x) dx$ is just one multiplication.

slides.text: $y = x^2 + 2x$ at $x = 3$ with $dx = 0.1$. Compute both.
slides.explain: $dy = 8(0.1) = 0.8$ and $Δy = 15.81 - 15 = 0.81$. Very close, and $dy$ was easier.

slides.text: A cube's side is measured as 5 cm, but the measurement could be off by 0.1 cm. Estimate how far off the volume $V = s^3$ could be.
slides.explain: $dV = 75(0.1) = 7.5$ cm³. A small error in the side becomes a bigger error in the volume.
slides.title: Estimating error
Wrap up
slides.text: Which of these are the linearization of $f$ at $a$?
slides.hint: Three of them are the same line written different ways.
slides.explain: All three are the tangent line. A linearization is not something new!

questions.text: The linearization of $f$ at $a$ is the tangent line to $f$ at $a$.
Match each piece of $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$ to its meaning.
pairs: height of the curve at the point

questions.text: $L(a)$ equals…
questions.explain: At $x = a$ the $(x - a)$ term is 0, so $L(a) = f(a)$. The line touches the curve there.

questions.text: The slope of $L(x)$ is…
Best choice of $a$ to approximate $sqrt(26)$:
questions.explain: 25 is close to 26 and $sqrt(25)$ = 5 is easy.

questions.text: Best choice of $a$ to approximate the cube root of 7.9:
questions.explain: The cube root of 8 is 2, and 8 is close.

questions.text: Best function and point to approximate $ln(1.04)$:
questions.explain: $ln 1 = 0$ and 1 is close to 1.04. ($ln 0$ doesn't exist.)

questions.text: Best function and point to approximate $e^(-0.03)$:
A linear approximation usually gets less accurate the farther $x$ is from $a$.
questions.explain: Near $a$ the curve hugs its tangent; far away they drift apart. Then make a new linearization.

questions.text: $f$ is concave up near $a$. Then $L(x)$ near $a$ is…
options: an underestimate (the tangent is below the curve)
an overestimate (the tangent is above the curve)
questions.explain: A concave-up curve bends up away from its tangent line, so the line sits below it.

questions.text: Match each quantity to its meaning.
questions.explain: $dy = f'(x) dx$ follows the tangent; $Δy$ follows the curve.

questions.text: If $y = x^3$, the differential $dy$ is…
questions.explain: $dy = f'(x) dx = 3x^2 dx$. (The last option is $Δy$.)

questions.text: If $y = sin x$, then $dy$ = …
$dy$ and $Δy$ are always exactly equal.
questions.explain: $dy$ is an approximation of $Δy$. They agree well only for small $dx$ (and exactly only if $f$ is a line).

questions.text: $dx$ and $Δx$ mean the same thing.
questions.explain: Both are the change in $x$ that you choose.

questions.text: A measurement of $x$ is off by $dx$. The error in $f(x)$ is approximately…
questions.explain: Error propagates like the differential: $dy = f'(x) dx$.

questions.text: Why use $dy$ instead of computing $Δy$?
options: $dy$ is just one multiplication; $Δy$ needs $f$ at a new point
questions.explain: Same reason as linearization: lines are easy.

questions.text: Which of these describe the linearization of $f$ at $a$?
questions.explain: It is the tangent line, and it is only trustworthy near $a$.

questions.explain: $f'(x) = sec^2 x$, which is 1 at 0. $L = 0 + (1)(0.05) ≈ 0.05$. (The real value is 0.050042.)
